citations.quote: Objectives: This paper provides a systematic literature review of DT applications in space robotics. The study aims to (i) classify primary objectives of their use, (ii) map applications across system lifecycle phases, (iii) identify recurring challenges, and (iv) report advantages while deriving analytical insights for future research.
RQ1: What are the primary objectives of using DTs in space robotics?
RQ2: What are the applications of DTs in space robotics?
RQ3: What are the current challenges and limitations of integrating DTs in space robotics?
RQ4: What are the advantages of using DTs in space robotics?

Building on these questions, our systematic literature review synthesizes the state of the art on DTs for space robotics by analyzing 46 peer-reviewed publications indexed in IEEE Xplore, ACM, and Scopus (covering studies up to the end of June 2024).
We covered all the studies from scratch till the end of June 2024.
Using this keyword, relevant papers were derived from the largest and most widely used scientific indexing systems and databases in software engineering: SCOPUS, IEEE Xplore Digital Library, and ACM.

As can be seen in Fig. 2, we conducted an automatic search on our objective datasets (Scopus, IEEE, and ACM) to retrieve studies aligned with our search string, from which a total of 2142 initial records were retrieved (Scopus: 1835; IEEE: 98; ACM: 209). Once we employed the inclusion and exclusion criteria 1403 papers remained (Scopus: 1237; IEEE: 90; ACM: 76).

They applied DT to monitor and control production processes, test different scenarios, optimize the assembly and integration of CubeSats before the actual physical implementation, provide data and bidirectional connection with the physical entity, detect faults, and enhance the robustness of the process.

Figueroa et al. [45] implemented a DT for the power manager system of the NASA Artemis Mission. They used the NASA Platform for Autonomous Systems electrical equipment domain libraries to create DT for fault diagnosis in the system.

DT applications in space robotics span the design, manufacturing, and service phases; however, they are unevenly distributed and predominantly phase-local. In the design phase, DTs are mainly used for iterative optimization and virtual verification of complex models. In manufacturing, they support production control, real-time monitoring, and quality management in smart assembly environments. In the service phase, DT implementations primarily focus on state monitoring, fault detection, and predictive maintenance.

Ensuring the accuracy and precision of DT models is challenging, particularly in manufacturing and path planning. High-quality data is essential for DTs to function effectively, but data collection and synchronizing data can be complex. Furthermore, integrating multiple DTs that interact with each other needs strong data consistency and network connectivity solutions. In addition, the development of reusable and general DT frameworks remains highly needed.

citations.quote: Beyond this distribution, a central systems engineering gap is the prevalence of phase-local DT solutions. In this review, most studies address exactly one lifecycle phase (40 out of 46), while only a small subset spans multiple phases (4 out of 46), and only two span all three phases.

Ground-only deployment dominates (35/46), with fewer hybrid ground/onboard instances (11/46) and no onboard-only cases in this corpus. Synchronization policies are predominantly continuous (22/46) and intermittent/batch (19/46), with few event-driven designs (5/46).

citations.quote: Research gaps. The reviewed literature highlights four main gaps. First, many DT implementations remain phase-local and do not support lifecycle continuity from design to operation. Second, validation under representative space conditions remains limited, especially for uncertain environments and delayed communication. Third, data availability and interoperability remain major barriers, particularly when proprietary design and production data are required. Fourth, reusable architectures and reporting standards are still missing, making it difficult to compare DT implementations across studies.

This synthesis is constrained by heterogeneity in DT definitions and evaluation practices across the reviewed studies. In particular, inconsistent reporting of coupling level, synchronization semantics, and validation realism limits strong causal inference.
Data will be made available on request.

Digital Twin technology is becoming a foundational capability for space robotics, but this study shows that today's evidence is still concentrated in a narrow set of use cases and validation settings. Most published works target either satellite/robot assembly and integration or the modeling and enhancement of robot behavior, where benefits are easier to measure and demonstrate.
Balancing fidelity vs. Complexity. Higher model fidelity can improve the usefulness of DTs, but it also increases computational cost, validation effort, and integration complexity.

The key goals of this phase are to (i) determine the importance of the work, (ii) outline exhaustive research goals and associated research questions, and (iii) develop research protocols that the researcher follows to conduct a systematic literature review.

Assurance and governance as engineering prerequisites: In space robotics, a DT is a decision-support subsystem (and sometimes a decision-generating subsystem). Therefore, requirements traceability, V&V evidence, uncertainty quantification (UQ), cybersecurity controls, and configuration management are not optional add-ons but enabling conditions for trust.

Leuter in [2] proposed a methodology to produce small satellites in orbit using AI approaches and DT. They presented a Digital Process Twin as a form of DT to map the processes without a fixed physical entity, unlike the original DT. They integrated two AI approaches into DPT to enable automated configuration and support assembly processes.
